title: Estimation from equal-width grouped data

parts.label: b

title: Comparing spread and detecting an outlier
stem: The five-number summaries for delivery times are A: (20,35,50,65,90) and B: (10,42,52,60,80), in minutes. The box plots share a scale.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Compare the medians and interquartile ranges.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Use the 1.5 IQR rule to test whether a new A delivery time of 120 minutes would be an outlier relative to the original A summary.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: A manager prioritizes consistency over the typical time. Explain which company these summaries support.

steps.text: Medians: A 50, B 52 minutes, so A has the smaller median.
IQR: A 30, B 18 minutes, so B has the smaller central spread.
120>110, so it would be an upper outlier.
B has the lower IQR, so its middle half is more consistent; this does not establish consistency for every delivery.

title: How an affine unit conversion changes summary statistics
stem: Temperatures measured in Celsius have mean 45, median 44 and standard deviation 6. Convert using $F=1.8C+32$. No assumption of a normal distribution is made.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Find the Fahrenheit mean and median.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Find the Fahrenheit standard deviation.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Find the Celsius temperature corresponding to 125 °F. Explain whether the fraction of observations above 125 °F can be determined from these summaries.

steps.text: A positive affine transformation preserves order and transforms the centre by the same formula.
Standard deviation scales by 1.8; adding 32 does not change spread.
The fraction cannot be determined: mean, median and standard deviation do not specify the full distribution.

title: A stratified sample and a response bias
stem: A school has 480 SL and 240 HL students. A survey will sample 60 students in proportion to course level. Separately, a voluntary online poll receives 50 SL and 70 HL responses.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Find the required SL and HL sample sizes for the stratified survey.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Compare the HL fraction in the voluntary poll with that in the school.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why random selection within each stratum is preferable for estimating the school-wide opinion.

steps.text: Poll HL fraction $70/120=7/12$; school HL fraction $1/3$.
Poll is 58.3% HL versus 33.3% in the school.
Random selection reduces self-selection bias within each level.
Proportional allocation represents the two levels correctly; the voluntary poll overrepresents HL and may also attract unusually motivated respondents.

title: Choosing the smallest batch for a success target

title: Why aggregate success rates can reverse a comparison
stem: A study compares methods A and B in two task groups. Easy tasks: A succeeds on 18 of 20; B on 80 of 100. Difficult tasks: A succeeds on 32 of 80; B on 8 of 20. Task allocation was not randomized.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Compare the success rates within each task group.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Find the aggregate success rate for each method.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why the aggregate comparison does not show B is the superior method.

steps.text: Combine successes and trial counts, rather than average the two percentages.
B is used much more often on easy tasks, while A is used mostly on difficult tasks.
Task difficulty confounds the aggregate comparison; a randomized or difficulty-balanced design is needed for a stronger comparison.
